analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act in its entirety, effective as if it had never passed.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act never received a House or Senate vote; it sat in committee for the entire two-year Congress with only one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act and its companion reconciliation law retroactively, restoring the health care rules that existed before 2010. That would end the ban on denying people with preexisting conditions, the subsidized coverage expansion, the Medicaid expansion, the closing of the Medicare drug-coverage gap, and the taxes that helped pay for it all, including a surtax on high incomes and fees on drug and device makers.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest gains would go to concentrated interests: high-income households, who would again avoid the 3.8% Medicare tax on investment income; brand-name drug makers and medical device manufacturers, whose ACA fees and taxes would disappear; and health insurers, freed from the requirement to cover preexisting conditions and from other market rules — though they would also lose the millions of subsidized customers the law created.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and the health care provisions of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, effective as of their enactment, restoring the law as if they had never been passed.
Revives or restores every provision of law that the ACA amended or repealed, unwinding the entire statutory structure rather than amending parts of it.

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions, who could again be denied coverage or charged more; the roughly 30 million people whose coverage came through the law's subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and young-adult provisions; seniors, who would again face the full Medicare drug-coverage gap; and low- and middle-income families losing premium tax credits.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions and subsidized coverage

drawbacks.text: Repeal would strip the law's core consumer protections — the ban on denying or charging more for preexisting conditions, premium subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, the dependent-coverage extension, and closure of the Medicare prescription-drug coverage gap — with no replacement coverage plan in the bill.

The bill would remove the law's funding mechanisms — including the high-income Medicare surtax and industry fees — without any offsetting way to pay for the health programs it keeps in place, adding to deficits.

Supporters argued the law's taxes and mandates burdened businesses and individuals; this bill addressed that by full repeal rather than targeted fixes, accepting the loss of the benefits above as the price.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gains flow mainly to high-income households and health industry companies through tax and fee repeal, while its costs fall on uninsured and sick people who gained coverage and protections under the ACA. It offered no replacement for the coverage it erased, so its benefits to concentrated interests are not balanced by comparable gains for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2011 and referred to eight House committees, which sent pieces of it to subcommittees, but none ever acted on it and no chamber ever voted, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Connie Mack introduced the bill on January 5, 2011, the opening day of the 112th Congress, with one Republican cosponsor.

The House referred it to eight full committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, Rules, and Appropriations — a referral pattern that requires every one of them to act before the bill can move.
Three subcommittees received portions of the bill in early 2011, and no committee or subcommittee took further action through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2013.
The bill never reached a floor vote in either the House or the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the repeal never advanced, the ACA's coverage protections, subsidies, and consumer rules remained in place, so people with preexisting conditions and subsidized coverage were better off; the high-income surtax and health industry fees it would have erased stayed in effect.

against.name: House committees of jurisdiction
against.role: Eight standing committees, including Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees but never reported it back for a floor vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its only cosponsor were both Republicans, and the bill attracted no Democratic support on its face; no vote occurred to measure the split.

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers from preexisting-condition and other market rules, but would also end the subsidized exchange customers and individual-mandate pool the law created. Their interest in shedding regulation ran against the sick people those rules protect.
Repeal would erase the ACA's fees on the pharmaceutical industry, shifting those costs back to taxpayers and beneficiaries.
Repeal would eliminate the ACA's tax on device sales, a cost the industry would no longer bear.
Repeal would end the Medicare tax on investment income above the high-income threshold, one of the law's main financing sources.

industries.industry: Newly insured low- and middle-income households
industries.note: Repeal would take away the premium subsidies and Medicaid expansion that extended coverage to millions.
